# An improved fast iterative moment method for the simulation of near-continuum gas flows with Shakhov model \(^\star\) Zhenning Caia, Zhicheng Hub,c,∗, Guanghan Lib,c, Chunwu Wangb,c, Xiaowen Wangb,c _a__Department of Mathematics, National University of Singapore, Level 4, Block S17, 10 Lower Kent Ridge Road, 119076, Singapore_ _b__School of Mathematics, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 211106, China_ _c__Key Laboratory of Mathematical Modelling and High Performance Computing of Air Vehicles (NUAA), Nanjing, 211106, China_ **Abstract** The fast iterative moment (FIM) method developed in [G. Li, C. Wang, and Z. Hu, Comput. Fluids, 311 (2026), 107031] achieves fast convergence for near-continuum gas flows modeled by the Boltzmann-BGK equation through alternating iterations between the high-order moment system and the consistent hydrodynamic equations. In this paper, we extend the FIM solver to the Shakhov model and improve it in the following aspects. A finite volume method with linear reconstruction is employed for high-resolution spatial discretization of both systems. Following the original FIM method, an implicit-explicit scheme treating the Shakhov collision term implicitly is adopted for the high-order moment system. A local Fourier analysis of a linearized one-dimensional BGK model reveals the need for more hydrodynamic iterations at smaller Knudsen numbers and their slower convergence on refined grids. Motivated by these findings, a Newton-multigrid method with a new regularization strategy is introduced for the hydrodynamic equations, generally providing an effective hydrodynamic correction with one step per alternating iteration, thereby reducing the need for empirical tuning. Numerical experiments for planar Couette flow, lid-driven cavity flow, and heat transfer in a bottom-heated cavity are carried out to investigate the performance of the improved FIM solver. The results demonstrate improved efficiency and robustness over the original FIM method, particularly at small Knudsen numbers, and favorable performance with both first- and second-order spatial discretizations. _Keywords:_ Boltzmann equation, Shakhov model, fast iterative moment method, linear reconstruction, Newton-multigrid method
_2000 MSC:_ 76P05, 65B99, 65M55 ### 1. Introduction In rarefied gas flows, the degree of gas rarefaction is characterized by the Knudsen number _Kn_, which is defined as the ratio between the mean free path \(\lambda\) of gas molecules and the characteristic flow length _L_. The Navier-Stokes-Fourier (NSF) equations based on the continuum fluid hypothesis are usually applicable up to _Kn_∼0.001 [1]. When _Kn_ is larger, the continuum hypothesis breaks down and the NSF equations fail to capture the non-conventional behaviour of the rarefied flow. To model rarefied gas dynamics accurately, mesoscopic kinetic models are generally adopted, among which the Boltzmann equation is the most fundamental one. However, despite the rapid development of modern high-performance computing, the numerical simulation of this equation remains computationally challenging due to its high dimensionality and nonlinear integro-differential structure. <tbc>with simplified relaxation terms, such as the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) model [2], the ellipsoidal statistical BGK (ES-BGK) model [3], and the Shakhov model [4]. Nevertheless, even with these simplified collision models, numerical simulation is still computationally demanding. In the past few decades, considerable effort has been devoted to developing efficient and accurate numerical methods for the Boltzmann equation and its simplified collision models; see, e.g., [5-10].

The moment method provides a hierarchy of macroscopic transport models capable of describing rarefaction effects beyond the NSF equations [11]. The method, originally proposed by Grad [12], approximates the distribution function by a Hermite expansion in velocity space with expansion parameters determined by the local physical quantities. When an appropriate closure ansatz is adopted [13, 14], the global hyperbolicity of moment systems of arbitrary order can be guaranteed. As the moment order increases, these systems often provide increasingly accurate approximations to the underlying Boltzmann equation [15, 16]. However, the rapidly increasing number of moment equations makes the direct formulation and implementation of high-order systems cumbersome. To address this issue, a unified numerical framework for high-order moment systems is developed in [7, 17, 18], where the full discretization can be formally obtained without explicitly writing out each equation. While this framework facilitates the practical implementation of high-order moment systems, efficiently computing their steady-state solutions remains challenging.

To accelerate the convergence of steady-state solutions of hyperbolic moment systems, we have previously developed two iterative solvers under the nonlinear multigrid (NMG) framework [19]: an NMG iteration using spatial coarse-grid corrections [20, 21] and a nonlinear multilevel moment (NMLM) iteration using lower-order model corrections [16, 22]. Both methods have shown significant improvement in convergence in comparison to the direct time-integration methods. However, the convergence of both methods still deteriorates significantly as _Kn_ decreases, leading to excessively high computational cost in the near-continuum flow regime. Moreover, integrating the two types of coarse-level corrections into a more efficient and robust multilevel solver remains nontrivial.

Motivated by the slow convergence of these methods in the near-continuum flow regime, we have developed a fast iterative moment (FIM) method in [23] by alternately solving the high-order moment system and the hydrodynamic equations with consistent constitutive relations and boundary conditions. Since the hydrodynamic equations constitute a subsystem of the moment system for \(M\ge 2\), they can efficiently predict the evolution of the primary macroscopic quantities at a much lower computational cost and thereby accelerate the overall iteration. This alternating framework can be further incorporated into the spatial NMG method, leading to an FIM-based multigrid solver that combines coarse-level corrections in the velocity and spatial spaces. From a broader perspective, the FIM method shares some conceptual similarities with several recently developed micro-macro acceleration methods, including the general synthetic iterative scheme (GSIS) [24], the unified gas-kinetic scheme (UGKS) [25], and the improved discrete velocity method (IDVM) [9, 26], although their formulations and implementations are fundamentally different.

Nevertheless, there is still room for improvement in the accuracy and efficiency of the FIM method. The original implementation is restricted to the Boltzmann-BGK equation and employs only first-order spatial discretization, which introduces considerable numerical dissipation and limits the spatial resolution. Moreover, the time-integration-based hydrodynamic solver in each alternating iteration usually requires a large number of iterations to sufficiently evolve the macroscopic quantities when _Kn_ is small. Its convergence may also slow down as the grid is refined, leading to increased computational cost for high-resolution simulations. Motivated by these limitations, in this work we extend the FIM solver to the Shakhov model, with the following main contributions.

• The spatial discretization is extended to second-order accuracy by employing a finite volume method with linear reconstruction for both the moment system and the consistent hydrodynamic equations.<tbc>

• An implicit-explicit (IMEX) scheme is adopted for the moment system, in which the Shakhov collision term is treated implicitly to improve numerical stability at small Knudsen numbers, as in the original FIM method for the BGK model.<tbc>

• A local Fourier analysis of a linearized one-dimensional BGK model is performed to explain the need for more hydrodynamic iterations at smaller Knudsen numbers and their slower convergence on refined grids.<tbc>

• A Newton-multigrid method equipped with a new regularization strategy is introduced for the hydrodynamic equations, replacing the time-integration-based methods used in [23].<tbc>

In general, one Newton-multigrid step per alternating iteration is sufficient to provide an effective hydrodynamic correction, substantially reducing the need for parameter tuning required in \[23\]. The resulting framework also provides an alternative way to integrate coarse-level corrections in the velocity and spatial spaces through the hydrodynamic equations and the Newton-multigrid method, respectively. With these improvements, the FIM solver achieves enhanced efficiency and robustness, particularly at small Knudsen numbers.

The rest of this paper is arranged as follows. In section 2, we introduce the model equations, their spatial discretization with linear reconstruction, and the FIM framework with the time-integration-based hydrodynamic solver. The local Fourier analysis is presented in section 3, and in section 4 both the IMEX scheme for the moment system with the Shakhov model and the Newton-multigrid method for the hydrodynamic equations are presented. Numerical experiments are carried out in section 5 to demonstrate the performance of the proposed method. Finally, some concluding remarks are given in the last section.

## 2. Governing equations and FIM framework

In this section, we first give a brief review of the steady-state Boltzmann-Shakhov equation and the high-order moment models, then present a unified spatial discretization with linear reconstruction for the given models, and finally introduce the FIM framework for solving the resulting discrete system.

### 2.1. Boltzmann equation with Shakhov collision term

The Boltzmann equation with a BGK-type collision term provides a fundamental description of gas flows in the near-continuum regime. For the steady-state problems considered in this work, it takes the form

\(v\cdot\nabla_xf=\bar{v}(f^\mathrm{E}-f).\) (1)

Here, _f_(**_x_**_,**v**_) is the distribution function, in which \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_D)\in\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^D\) (_D_=1,2 or 3) and \(v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)\in\mathbb{R}^3\) represent the spatial location and velocity of the gas molecules, respectively. The left-hand side of (1) describes the change of _f_ due to the free streaming, while the right-hand side models the interactions between gas molecules via a simplified relaxation process. The average collision frequency \(\bar{v}\) determines how fast the distribution function approaches equilibrium, assumed to be independent of **_v_** and inversely proportional to the Knudsen number, i.e., \(\bar{v}\propto 1/Kn\). In the BGK model, the function _f_<sup>E</sup> equals the local Maxwellian _f_<sup>M</sup> defined by

\(f^\mathcal{M}(x,v)=\frac{\rho(x)}{m_*(2\pi\theta(x))^{3/2}}\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{|v-u(x)|^2}{2\theta(x)}\right),\) (2)

where _m_<sub>∗</sub> is the mass of a single gas molecule. The macroscopic quantities in (2), including the mass density \(\rho(x)\), the mean velocity **_u_**(**_x_**)=(_u_<sub>1</sub>_,u_<sub>2</sub>_,u_<sub>3</sub>) and the temperature \(\theta(x)\), can be computed from the distribution function _f_ as

\(\rho(x)=m_*\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f(x,v)\mathrm{d}v,\rho(x)u(x)=m_*\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}vf(x,v)\mathrm{d}v,\rho(x)|u(x)|^2+3\rho(x)\theta(x)=m_*\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|v|^2f(x,v)\mathrm{d}v.\) (3)

It is well known that the BGK model does not produce the correct Prandtl number. A commonly used fix is the Shakhov model \[4\], in which the equilibrium distribution _f_<sup>E</sup> is given by<tbc>

\(f^\mathrm{E}(x,v)=\left[1+\frac{(1-\mathrm{Pr})(v-u(x))\cdot q(x)}{5\rho(x)[\theta(x)]^2}\left(\frac{|v-u(x)|^2}{\theta(x)}-5\right)\right]f^\mathcal{M}(x,v),\) (4)

<tbc>where the Prandtl number can be specified by the parameter Pr, and **_q_** denotes the heat flux of the gas to be defined later. When Pr=1, the Shakhov model reduces to the BGK model. The nonequilibrium moments, including the stress tensor \(\sigma_{ij}\), _i,j_=1,2,3, and the heat flux **_q_**, can be computed from the distribution function as

\(\sigma_{ij}(x)=m_*\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}(v_i-u_i(x))(v_j-u_j(x))f(x,v)\mathrm{d}v-\rho(x)\theta(x)\delta_{ij},i,j=1,2,3,q(x)=\frac{m_*}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|v-u(x)|^2(v-u(x))f(x,v)\mathrm{d}v.\text{(5)}\)

Here \(\delta_{ij}\) is Kronecker’s delta symbol. Note that \(\sigma_{ij}\) is a trace-free tensor satisfying \(\sigma_{11}+\sigma_{22}+\sigma_{33}=0\).

## 2.2. High-order hyperbolic moment system and hydrodynamic equations

To obtain moment models for the Boltzmann equation (1), the distribution function is first expanded into a series of Hermite functions as<tbc>

\(f(x,v)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^3}f_\alpha(x)\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[\varpi,\vartheta]}(v),\) (6)

<tbc>where \(f_\alpha(x)\) are the coefficients, and \(\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[\varpi,\vartheta]}(\cdot)\) are the basis functions defined by<tbc>

\(\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[\varpi,\vartheta]}(v)=\frac{1}{m_*(2\pi\vartheta)^{3/2}\vartheta^{|\alpha|/2}}\prod_{d=1}^3He_{\alpha_d}(\xi_d)\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{\xi_d^2}{2}\right),\xi=\frac{v-\varpi}{\sqrt{\vartheta}},\forall v\in\mathbb{R}^3.\)

<tbc>In the above expression, \(\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)\) is a multi-index with order \(|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3\), and \(He_n(\cdot)\) is the Hermite polynomial of degree _n_ given by<tbc>

\(He_n(x)=(-1)^n\mathrm{exp}\left(\frac{x^2}{2}\right)\frac{\mathrm{d}^n}{\mathrm{d}x^n}\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{x^2}{2}\right).\)

<tbc>The parameters \(\varpi\in\mathbb{R}^3\) and \(\vartheta\in\mathbb{R}^+\) in the basis function could be either constants as in the Hermite spectral method \[27\], or variables depending on **_x_**. In Grad’s moment method \[12\], \(\varpi\) and \(\vartheta\) are chosen adaptively as the local mean velocity **_u_** and the local temperature \(\theta\), which are determined from _f_ itself via (3). With this choice, the relationship between the moment coefficients \(f_\alpha\) and the macroscopic variables can be deduced from (3) and (5) as

\(f_0=\rho,f_{e_1}=f_{e_2}=f_{e_3}=0,\sum_{d=1}^3f_{2e_d}=0,\sigma_{ij}=(1+\delta_{ij})f_{e_i+e_j},q_i=2f_{3e_i}+\sum_{d=1}^3f_{2e_d+e_i},i,j=1,2,3,\text{(7)}\)

where _e_<sub>1</sub>, _e_<sub>2</sub>, _e_<sub>3</sub> represent the multi-indices (1,0,0), (0,1,0) and (0,0,1), respectively. Since the first term of series (6) already recovers the local Maxwellian, Grad’s method often provides an efficient approximation of the distribution function for flows close to thermodynamic equilibrium. Accordingly, we adopt Grad’s choice \(\varpi=u\) and \(\vartheta=\theta\) for the representation of the distribution function in the near-continuum flow regime considered in this paper.

Numerically, the distribution function is approximated by a truncated series of order _M_, that is,<tbc>

\(f(x,v)\approx\sum_{|\alpha|\le M}f_\alpha(x)\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[u,\vartheta]}(v)\in\mathcal{F}_M^{[u,\theta]},\) (8)

<tbc>in which \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u,\theta]}\) is the linear space spanned by the basis functions \(\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[u,\vartheta]}(v)\) with \(|\alpha|\le M\). Substituting the expansion (8) into the Boltzmann equation (1) and following the procedures in \[13, 17, 28\], we obtain the globally hyperbolic moment system of order _M_. With \(\varrho\) denoting the vector of all independent variables **_u_**, \(\theta\), and \(f_\alpha\) with \(|\alpha|\le M\), the resulting system can be written in the quasi-linear form

\(\sum_{d=1}^D\mathbf{A}_d(\varrho)\frac{\partial\varrho}{\partial x_d}=\mathcal{Q}(\varrho),\) (9)

where the left-hand side is derived from the convection part of the Boltzmann equation, and the right-hand side corresponds to the collision term. The detailed expression of the above system can be found for the Boltzmann- Shakhov equation in Appendix A. For \(M\ge 2\), the factor 1_/Kn_ enters the right-hand side of (9) through the collision frequency \(\bar{v}\), making the system increasingly stiff as \(Kn\rightarrow 0\).

Moreover, the conservation laws of mass, momentum and energy form a natural subsystem of the moment system (9) for \(M\ge 2\). The corresponding hydrodynamic equations for the primary macroscopic quantities \(\rho\), **_u_** and \(\theta\) take the<tbc>

form

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c }
\nabla_x\cdot(\rho u)=0, \\
\nabla_x\cdot(\rho u\otimes u+p\mathbf{I}+\sigma)=0, \\
\nabla_x\cdot(\rho Eu+pu+u\cdot\sigma+q)=0,
\end{array}\right.\) (10)

where \(p=\rho\theta\) is the pressure, **I** is the identity matrix, and \(E=3\theta/2+|u|^2/2\) is the specific total energy.

## 2.3. Spatial discretization of the moment system and linear reconstruction

The hyperbolic moment system (9) of order _M_ is discretized following the unified finite volume method developed in \[7, 17, 18, 29\]. For convenience, only the one-dimensional formulation is presented here, while the extension to two-dimensional problems on rectangular grids is straightforward.

Suppose the spatial domain \(\Omega=(x_L,x_R)\) is partitioned into _N<sub>x</sub>_ uniform grid cells of size \(\Delta x\), where the _i_th cell is denoted by K_<sub>i</sub>_=\[_x_<sub>_i_-1/2</sub>_,x_<sub>_i_+1/2</sub>\]. In each cell K_<sub>i</sub>_, we use _f<sub>i</sub>_(**_v_**) and \(f_i^\pm(v)\) to denote the cell-averaged distribution function and the reconstructed interface distribution functions at \(x_{i\pm 1/2}\), respectively. Then the finite volume discretization of the Boltzmann equation (1) is given by<tbc>

\(-\frac{1}{\Delta x}\left(\bar{F}_{i+1/2}\left(f_i^+,f_{i+1}^-\right)-\bar{F}_{i-1/2}\left(f_{i-1}^+,f_i^-\right)\right)+\mathcal{Q}(f_i)=0.\) (11)

<tbc>Here, \(\bar{F}_{i\pm 1/2}\left(\cdot,\cdot\right)\) are the numerical fluxes at the boundaries of the _i_th grid cell, and Q(_f<sub>i</sub>_) denotes the collision term evaluated using the cell-averaged distribution function _f<sub>i</sub>_. Let us assume that _f<sub>i</sub>_(**_v_**) belongs to the function space \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u_i,\theta_i]}\), i.e.,<tbc>

\(f_i(v)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le M}f_{i,\alpha}\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[u_i,\theta_i]}(v),\) (12)

<tbc>where **_u_**_<sub>i</sub>_ and \(\theta_i\) are the local mean velocity and temperature, respectively, so that the relations (7) hold for the coefficients \(f_{i,\alpha}\). Similarly, the numerical fluxes \(\bar{F}_{i\pm 1/2}\left(\cdot,\cdot\right)\) and the collision term Q(_f<sub>i</sub>_) in (11) should be expressed as functions in the same space \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u_i,\theta_i]}\) as follows

\(\bar{F}_{i\pm 1/2}\left(\cdot,\cdot\right)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le M}\bar{F}_{i\pm 1/2,\alpha}\left(\cdot,\cdot\right)\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[u_i,\theta_i]}(v),\mathcal{Q}(f_i)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le M}\mathcal{Q}_{i,\alpha}\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[u_i,\theta_i]}(v),\) (13)

where \(\bar{F}_{i\pm 1/2,\alpha}\left(\cdot,\cdot\right)\) and \(\mathcal{Q}_{i,\alpha}\) are the coefficients. Substituting the expansions (12) and (13) into the system (11) and matching the coefficients of the same basis function \(\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[u_i,\theta_i]}(v)\), we obtain the finite volume discretization for the hyperbolic moment system (9).

In the present numerical experiments, a modified Harten, Lax and van Leer (HLL) flux, as used in \[18\], is adopted for \(\bar{F}_{i\pm 1/2}\left(\cdot,\cdot\right)\). In order to write the numerical flux in the form (13), all distribution functions involved in (11), including those in neighboring grid cells, need to be represented as members of \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u_i,\theta_i]}\). This requires a projection onto \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u_i,\theta_i]}\) for any function in \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[\varpi,\vartheta]}\) if \(\varpi\neq u_i\) or \(\vartheta\neq\theta_i\), regardless of the choice of the numerical flux. An efficient implementation of the required projection, which preserves all moments up to the _M_th order, can be found in \[27\].

It remains to determine the distribution functions on cell boundaries \(f_i^-\) and \(f_i^+\), which are to be constructed as functions in \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u_i^\cdot,\theta_i^-]}\) and \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u_i^\cdot,\theta_i^+]}\). Obviously, it is equivalent to determine the parameters \(u_i^\pm\), \(\theta_i^\pm\) and all coefficients \(f_{i,\alpha}^\pm\) with \(|\alpha|\le M\). In our method, we first calculate the reconstructed vectors of conservative variables on the cell boundaries as<tbc>

\(U_i^+=U_i+\frac{\Delta x}{2}s_i,U_i^-=U_i-\frac{\Delta x}{2}s_i,\) (14)

<tbc>where \(U_i=[\rho_i,\rho_iu_i,\rho_iE_i]^\mathsf{T}\) is the vector on the _i_th cell. The parameters \(u_i^\pm\) and \(\theta_i^\pm\) are then extracted from \(U_i^\pm\). Following \[21, 22\], the coefficients are reconstructed as<tbc>

\(f_{i,\alpha}^+=f_{i,\alpha}+\frac{\Delta x}{2}d_{i,\alpha},f_{i,\alpha}^-=f_{i,\alpha}-\frac{\Delta x}{2}d_{i,\alpha}.\) (15)

A first-order scheme can be obtained by setting all slopes **_s_**_<sub>i</sub>_ and \(d_{i,\alpha}\) to 0, while a second-order discretization is achieved by employing

\(s_i=\frac{U_{i+1}-U_{i-1}}{2\Delta x},d_{i,\alpha}=\frac{f_{i+1,\alpha}-f_{i-1,\alpha}}{2\Delta x}.\) (16)

Finally, appropriate boundary conditions are necessary to complete the discretization. The Maxwell boundary condition is employed throughout our numerical experiments. We refer to \[17, 18\] for details on such boundary conditions.

## 2.4. FIM framework

For convenience, the discretization (11) over the _i_th cell is rewritten in the residual form<tbc>

\(\mathcal{R}_i(f)=0,\) (17)

<tbc>where R_<sub>i</sub>_(**_f_**) denotes the local residual corresponding to the left-hand side of (11), and **_f_** is the global vector composed of all cell-averaged distribution functions _f<sub>i</sub>_. The above discretization results in a nonlinear system coupling all unknowns, including **_u_**_<sub>i</sub>_, \(\theta_i\), and \(f_{i,\alpha}\) for _i_=0,1_,...,N<sub>x</sub>_-1 and \(|\alpha|\le M\). A simple relaxation method for solving this nonlinear system is the Richardson iteration given by<tbc>

\(f_i^{n+1}=f_i^n+\omega\mathcal{R}_i\left(f^n\right),\) (18)

<tbc>where the superscript _n_ is the index for iteration steps. The relaxation parameter \(\omega\) is selected according to the CFL condition<tbc>

\(\omega=min_i\omega_i,\) (19)

<tbc>where the local relaxation parameter \(\omega_i\) satisfies

\(\omega_i\left(\frac{|u_{i,1}^n|+C_{M+1}\sqrt{\theta_i^n}}{\Delta x}\right)<1.\) (20)

Here, \(u_{i,1}^n\) is the first component of the vector \(u_i^n\), and _C_<sub>_M_+1</sub> is the maximal root of the Hermite polynomial of degree _M_+1. Under Grad’s expansion, the left- and right-hand sides of (18) are represented in different function spaces, namely, \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u_i^{n+1},\theta_i^{n+1}]}\) and \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u_i^n,\theta_i^n]}\), respectively. Therefore, the evaluated right-hand side should be projected onto \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u_i^{n+1},\theta_i^{n+1}]}\) using the projection mentioned in the previous subsection. The Richardson iteration (18) can be interpreted as an explicit Euler scheme with the relaxation parameter \(\omega\) serving as the pseudo-time step. As _Kn_ decreases, its convergence becomes increasingly slower, resulting in poor efficiency in the near-continuum flow regime.

To accelerate the convergence, the FIM method proposed in \[23\] employs an alternating iteration framework consisting of a moment stage for the high-order moment system (9) and a hydrodynamic stage for the hydrodynamic equations (10). Specifically, in the moment stage, \(\gamma_1\) moment iterations are performed starting from the current moment solution **_f_**_<sup>n</sup>_ to obtain an intermediate approximation \(\tilde{f}\). In the hydrodynamic stage, using the macroscopic quantities \(\tilde{\rho}\), \(\tilde{u}\), and \(\tilde{\theta}\) extracted from \(\tilde{f}\) as the initial guess, at most \(\gamma_2\) hydrodynamic iterations are performed. The resulting macroscopic solution is subsequently used to update \(\tilde{f}\) and construct the new moment solution **_f_**<sup>_n_+1</sup>. The above procedure is summarized in **Algorithm 1**. In \[23\], the Richardson iteration (18) or its symmetric Gauss-Seidel (SGS) version is used in the moment stage, while a similar iterative scheme with a consistent spatial discretization is employed in the hydrodynamic stage, as described below.

Let _U<sub>i</sub>_ represent the cell average of _U_ over the _i_th grid cell R_<sub>i</sub>_. Applying the finite volume method to (10) gives<tbc>

\(\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}(U):=-\frac{1}{\Delta x}\left[\hat{F}_{i+1/2}\left(U_i^+,U_{i+1}^-,\sigma_i^+,\sigma_{i+1}^-,q_i^+,q_{i+1}^-\right)-\hat{F}_{i-1/2}\left(U_{i-1}^+,U_i^-,\sigma_{i-1}^+,\sigma_i^-,q_{i-1}^+,q_i^-\right)\right]=0,\) (21)

<tbc>where \(\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}(U)\) denotes the local hydrodynamic residual, **_U_** consists of all cell averages _U<sub>i</sub>_, and \(U_i^\pm\) are reconstructed according to (14). Similarly, the interface values of the stress tensor \(\sigma\) and heat flux **_q_** are reconstructed as<tbc>

\(\sigma_i^+=\tilde{\sigma}_i+\frac{\Delta x}{2}\tilde{s}_i,\sigma_i^-=\tilde{\sigma}_i-\frac{\Delta x}{2}\tilde{s}_i,q_i^+=\tilde{q}_i+\frac{\Delta x}{2}\tilde{s}_i,q_i^-=\tilde{q}_i-\frac{\Delta x}{2}\tilde{s}_i,\) (22)

**Algorithm 1** One step of the FIM alternating iteration \[23\]

**Input:** Grid, **_f_**_<sup>n</sup>_

**Output:** The new approximation **_f_**<sup>_n_+1</sup> denoted by **_f_**<sup>_n_+1</sup>=FIM\(\big(\)**_f_**_<sup>n</sup>_\(\big)\)

1: Perform \(\gamma_1\) moment iterations for (9) to obtain a new approximation \(\tilde{f}\) from **_f_**_<sup>n</sup>_;

2: Compute \(\tilde{\rho}\), \(\tilde{u}\) and \(\tilde{\theta}\) on all grid cells from \(\tilde{f}\);

3: Prepare hydrodynamic initial guess **_U_**<sup>0</sup> with \(U_i^0=\left[\tilde{\rho}_i,\tilde{\rho}_i\tilde{u}_i,\frac{1}{2}\tilde{\rho}_i\left(3\tilde{\theta}_i+|\tilde{u}_i|^2\right)\right]^\mathrm{T}\) and set _m_=0;

4: Calculate **_U_**<sup>_m_+1</sup> from **_U_**_<sup>m</sup>_ by performing one hydrodynamic iteration for (10) with compatible constitutive relations \(\sigma\), **_q_** and boundary conditions. If \((m+1)\ge\gamma_2\) or \(\|U^{m+1}-U^m\|_1\le tol\), then break; otherwise, let _m_:=_m_+1, and repeat the current step;

5: Extract \(\rho^{m+1}\), **_u_**<sup>_m_+1</sup> and \(\theta^{m+1}\) from **_U_**<sup>_m_+1</sup>;

6: Construct **_f_**<sup>_n_+1</sup> from \(\tilde{f}\) by replacing \(\tilde{\rho}\), \(\tilde{u}\) and \(\tilde{\theta}\) with \(\rho^{m+1}\), **_u_**<sup>_m_+1</sup> and \(\theta^{m+1}\), respectively.

<tbc>where \(\tilde{\sigma}_i\) and \(\tilde{q}_i\) are evaluated from the intermediate moment solution \(\tilde{f}\). The slopes vanish for the first-order discretization, while for the second-order discretization they are given by

\(\tilde{s}_i=\frac{\tilde{\sigma}_{i+1}-\tilde{\sigma}_{i-1}}{2\Delta x},\tilde{s}_i=\frac{\tilde{q}_{i+1}-\tilde{q}_{i-1}}{2\Delta x},\) (23)

where \(\tilde{\sigma}_{i\pm 1}\) and \(\tilde{q}_{i\pm 1}\) are also evaluated from \(\tilde{f}\) on the neighboring cells. The spatial discretization of the hydrodynamic equations is required to be consistent with that of the moment system, including the reconstruction procedure, numerical fluxes, and characteristic wave speeds used in the HLL flux.

In \[23\], the boundary conditions for the hydrodynamic equations are obtained indirectly from the distribution- function boundary treatment of the moment system. In the present method, the ghost-cell values for the hydrodynamic equations are instead obtained directly from the explicit expressions given in Appendix B, thereby simplifying the boundary treatment.

The discrete system (21) can be solved using the Richardson iteration given by

\(U_i^{m+1}=U_i^m+\omega\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}\left(U^m\right),\) (24)

where the relaxation parameter \(\omega\) is again determined by the CFL condition given in (19) and (20). Here, the superscript _m_ corresponds to the iterations for solving the hydrodynamic equations. To improve convergence, the SGS method can be incorporated into (24), yielding

\(U_i^{m+1}=U_i^m+\omega_i\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}\left(U^*\right),\) (25)

where **_U_**<sup>∗</sup> is a vector initialized with **_U_**_<sup>m</sup>_ and updated cell by cell as the new approximation \(U_i^{m+1}\) becomes available during the sweep. For convenience, this SGS iteration is referred to as the Hydro-SGS iteration hereafter.

Numerical experiments in \[23\] indicate that \(\gamma_1\) is often set to 1 or 2 in practice, while \(\gamma_2\) needs to be chosen appropriately to balance the per-iteration cost and the overall convergence rate. When _Kn_ becomes small, \(\gamma_2\) usually needs to be increased to tens or even hundreds to ensure that the hydrodynamic information is sufficiently captured. Replacing the Richardson iteration (24) with Hydro-SGS can improve the convergence of the hydrodynamic solver, but a relatively large \(\gamma_2\) is still required.

## 3. Convergence analysis of the FIM method

One hydrodynamic iteration (24) or (25) is usually faster than one moment iteration due to the smaller number of unknowns. However, a large \(\gamma_2\), which is often required at small _Kn_ \[23\], increases the computational cost of the hydrodynamic stage in each alternating iteration and may reduce the overall efficiency of the FIM method. In order to better understand this behavior and motivate further improvements, we analyze the convergence of the FIM method in the near-continuum regime based on a linearized one-dimensional BGK model. This simplified model retains the essential coupling between the primary macroscopic quantities and nonequilibrium moments while allowing an explicit local Fourier analysis. This section summarizes the main results, while the detailed derivations are provided in Appendix C.

## 3.1. Linearized model and the fast iterative method

Following \[30\], the moment equations for the linearized one-dimensional BGK model take the form

\(\mathbf{A}\frac{du}{dx}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\mathbf{Lu},\mathbf{u}=(u_0,u_1,\dots,u_M)^\mathsf{T},\varepsilon=\text{Kn},\) (26)

where \(M\ge 3\) and

\(\mathbf{A}=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c c c }
0 & 1 &  &  &  &  \\
1 & 0 & 2 &  &  &  \\
1 & \ddots & \ddots &  &  &  \\
 & \ddots & \ddots & M &  &  \\
 &  &  & 1 & 0
\end{array}\right),\mathbf{L}=\text{diag}(0,0,0,-1,\dots,-1).\) (27)

The first three rows of (26), describing the evolution of the primary macroscopic quantities, are

\(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\mathbf{A}_hU+\mathbf{b}u_3\right)=\mathbf{0},\) (28)

where

\(\mathbf{U}=\left(u_0,u_1,u_2\right)^\mathsf{T},\mathbf{A}_h=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c }
0 & 1 & 0 \\
1 & 0 & 2 \\
0 & 1 & 0
\end{array}\right),\mathbf{b}=\left(\begin{array}{ c }
0 \\
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right).\) (29)

With first-order spatial discretization using the HLL flux, the moment system (26) becomes

\(\frac{\mathbf{A}}{2\Delta x}\left(\mathbf{u}_{j+1}-\mathbf{u}_{j-1}\right)-\frac{C_{M+1}}{2\Delta x}\left(\mathbf{u}_{j+1}-2\mathbf{u}_j+\mathbf{u}_{j-1}\right)=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\mathbf{Lu}_j.\) (30)

The corresponding discretization of (28) is given by the first three rows of this system, with _u_<sub>3</sub> held fixed during the hydrodynamic stage.

We focus on the FIM method for (30), with SGS iterations applied to both the moment and hydrodynamic stages, and assume that the relaxation parameter \(\omega\) is independent of \(\varepsilon\). Define \(\nu=\omega C_{M+1}/\Delta x\) with \(0<\nu<1\), and let \(\mathbf{u}_j^{(n)}\) be the approximate solution in the _j_th grid cell after _n_ FIM iterations. The next FIM iteration is defined by the following steps:

1. Moment SGS: \(\gamma_1\) implicit-explicit SGS (IMEX-SGS) iterations in the moment stage, defined by<tbc>

• Initialize \(\mathbf{u}_j^{(n,0)}=\mathbf{u}_j^{(n)}\), then perform the following two sweeps for each \(s=0,1,\dots,\gamma_1-1\):<tbc>

• Forward sweep: in increasing order of _j_, solve for \(\mathbf{u}_j^{(n,s+1/2)}\) from<tbc>

\(\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\omega}{\varepsilon}\mathbf{L}\right)\mathbf{u}_j^{(n,s+1/2)}=(1-\nu)\mathbf{u}_j^{(n,s)}+\frac{\nu}{2}\left(\mathbf{I}+\frac{\mathbf{A}}{C_{M+1}}\right)\mathbf{u}_{j-1}^{(n,s+1/2)}+\frac{\nu}{2}\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\mathbf{A}}{C_{M+1}}\right)\mathbf{u}_{j+1}^{(n,s)};\) \(\text{(31)}\)

• Backward sweep: in decreasing order of _j_, solve for \(\mathbf{u}_j^{(n,s+1)}\) from<tbc>

\(\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\omega}{\varepsilon}\mathbf{L}\right)\mathbf{u}_j^{(n,s+1)}=(1-\nu)\mathbf{u}_j^{(n,s+1/2)}+\frac{\nu}{2}\left(\mathbf{I}+\frac{\mathbf{A}}{C_{M+1}}\right)\mathbf{u}_{j-1}^{(n,s+1/2)}+\frac{\nu}{2}\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\mathbf{A}}{C_{M+1}}\right)\mathbf{u}_{j+1}^{(n,s+1)}.\) \(\text{(32)}\)

2. Hydrodynamic SGS: \(\gamma_2\) Hydro-SGS iterations in the hydrodynamic stage, defined by<tbc>

• Set \(\mathbf{U}_j^{(n,0)}=(\mathbf{u}_{j,0}^{(n,\gamma_1)},\mathbf{u}_{j,1}^{(n,\gamma_1)},\mathbf{u}_{j,2}^{(n,\gamma_1)})^\mathsf{T}\), then perform the following two sweeps for each \(\ell=0,1,\dots,\gamma_2-1\):<tbc>

• Forward sweep: in increasing order of _j_, solve for \(\mathbf{U}_j^{(n,\ell+1/2)}\) from<tbc>

\(\mathbf{U}_j^{(n,\ell+1/2)}=(1-\nu)\mathbf{U}_j^{(n,\ell)}+\frac{\nu}{2}\left(\mathbf{I}+\frac{\mathbf{A}_h}{C_{M+1}}\right)\mathbf{U}_{j-1}^{(n,\ell+1/2)}+\frac{\nu}{2}\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\mathbf{A}_h}{C_{M+1}}\right)\mathbf{U}_{j+1}^{(n,\ell)}-\frac{\nu}{2C_{M+1}}\mathbf{b}\left(\mathbf{u}_{j+1,3}^{(n,\gamma_1)}-\mathbf{u}_{j-1,3}^{(n,\gamma_1)}\right);\) \(\text{(33)}\)

• Backward sweep: in decreasing order of _j_, solve for \(\mathbf{U}_j^{(n,\ell+1)}\) from<tbc>

\(\mathbf{U}_j^{(n,\ell+1)}=(1-\nu)\mathbf{U}_j^{(n,\ell+1/2)}+\frac{\nu}{2}\left(\mathbf{I}+\frac{\mathbf{A}_h}{C_{M+1}}\right)\mathbf{U}_{j-1}^{(n,\ell+1/2)}+\frac{\nu}{2}\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\mathbf{A}_h}{C_{M+1}}\right)\mathbf{U}_{j+1}^{(n,\ell+1)}-\frac{\nu}{2C_{M+1}}\mathbf{b}\left(u_{j+1,3}^{(n,\gamma_1)}-u_{j-1,3}^{(n,\gamma_1)}\right).\) \(\text{(34)}\)

3. The solution after the (_n_+1)th FIM iteration is then given by

\(\mathbf{u}_j^{(n+1)}=\left((\mathbf{U}_j^{(n,\gamma_2)})^\mathsf{T},u_{j,3}^{(n,\gamma_1)},u_{j,4}^{(n,\gamma_1)},\dots,u_{j,M}^{(n,\gamma_1)}\right)^\mathsf{T}.\) \(\text{(35)}\)

The results of the Fourier analysis of this numerical method are presented in the next subsection.

## 3.2. Results of the Fourier analysis and low-frequency behavior

Define the error after _n_ FIM iterations by<tbc>

\(\delta\mathbf{u}_j^{(n)}=\mathbf{u}_j^{(n)}-\mathbf{u}_j,\) (36)

<tbc>where **_u_**_<sub>j</sub>_ is the exact solution of the discrete system (30). We neglect boundary effects associated with the sweeps and assume that the solution is periodic in space with period \(2\pi\). Consider a Fourier mode of the form<tbc>

\(\delta\mathbf{u}_j^{(n)}=\widehat{\mathbf{e}}^{(n)}(k)e^{\mathrm{i}jk\Delta x},\widehat{\mathbf{e}}^{(n)}(k)\in\mathbb{C}^{M+1}.\) (37)

<tbc>Since the numerical scheme is linear, we define its Fourier error-propagation matrix \(\mathbf{T}(\varepsilon,k)\) by

\(\widehat{\mathbf{e}}^{(n+1)}(k)=\mathbf{T}(\varepsilon,k)\widehat{\mathbf{e}}^{(n)}(k),\mathbf{T}(\varepsilon,k)\in\mathbb{C}^{(M+1)\times(M+1)}.\) (38)

The maximum magnitude of the amplification factors is given by the spectral radius of \(\mathbf{T}(\varepsilon,k)\).

As shown in Appendix C.3, at most three eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{T}(\varepsilon,k)\) have _O_(1) leading terms in the near-continuum limit \(\varepsilon\rightarrow 0\). They are indexed by \(\mu\in\{-\sqrt{3},0,\sqrt{3}\}\), the eigenvalues of **A**_<sub>h</sub>_, and can be expanded as

\(\Lambda_\mu(\varepsilon,k)=\Lambda_\mu^{(0)}(k)+\varepsilon\Lambda_\mu^{(1)}(k)+O(\varepsilon^2).\) (39)

The remaining _M_-2 eigenvalues have magnitudes of \(O(\varepsilon)\) and are therefore negligible in the near-continuum limit. For the three branches in (39), define

\(\mathcal{G}_\mu^{(0)}(k)=\frac{\left[1-\nu+\frac{\nu}{2}\left(1-\frac{\mu}{C_{M+1}}\right)e^{\mathrm{i}k\Delta x}\right]\left[1-\nu+\frac{\nu}{2}\left(1+\frac{\mu}{C_{M+1}}\right)e^{-\mathrm{i}k\Delta x}\right]}{\left[1-\frac{\nu}{2}\left(1+\frac{\mu}{C_{M+1}}\right)e^{-\mathrm{i}k\Delta x}\right]\left[1-\frac{\nu}{2}\left(1-\frac{\mu}{C_{M+1}}\right)e^{\mathrm{i}k\Delta x}\right]}.\) (40)

Their leading amplification factors are

\(\Lambda_\mu^{(0)}(k)=\left[\mathcal{G}_\mu^{(0)}(k)\right]^{\gamma_1+\gamma_2},\mu\in\{-\sqrt{3},0,\sqrt{3}\}.\) (41)

When \(\gamma_1=1\), the first-order term \(\Lambda_\mu^{(1)}(k)\) has also been derived. Due to its complexity, we refer readers to Appendix C.5 (equation (C.46)) for its expression.

It can be shown that \(|\mathcal{G}_\mu^{(0)}(k)|\) attains its maximum value of 1 at _k_=0 for all \(\mu\in\{-\sqrt{3},0,\sqrt{3}\}\) (see Proposition 1). Meanwhile, when \(|k\Delta x|<2\pi/5\), we have \(|\mathcal{G}_0^{(0)}(k)|\ge|\mathcal{G}_{\pm\sqrt{3}}^{(0)}(k)|\) (see Proposition 2). Therefore, we will mainly focus on the case \(\mu=0\) and small nonzero values of \(|k\Delta x|\). In this case, we have<tbc>

\(\Lambda_0^{(0)}(k)=\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{2\nu}{2-\nu}(\gamma_1+\gamma_2)k^2\Delta x^2\right)+O\left((k\Delta x)^4\right).\)

<tbc>This result is consistent with the well-known smoothing property of the SGS method, indicating that the number of sweeps required to reduce a fixed low-frequency error mode by a constant factor should scale as \(\Delta x^{-2}\) for fixed \(\nu\). It also shows the benefit of the FIM method: when \(\varepsilon\) is small, one can increase \(\gamma_2\) while reducing \(\gamma_1\), keeping their<tbc>

sum fixed, without affecting the leading-order convergence factor. This reduces the computational cost because the hydrodynamic stage is much less expensive than the moment stage.

However, this does not explain the observation in \[23\] that a larger \(\gamma_2\) is required when the Knudsen number is smaller. To understand this, we consider the first-order term \(\Lambda_0^{(1)}(k)\) for \(\gamma_1=1\). Since \(\Lambda_0^{(0)}(k)\ge 0\), we have

\(|\Lambda_0(\varepsilon,k)|^2=|\Lambda_0^{(0)}(k)|^2+2\varepsilon\Lambda_0^{(0)}(k)\mathrm{Re}\Lambda_0^{(1)}(k)+O(\varepsilon^2),\)

and therefore, it suffices to study the real part of \(\Lambda_0^{(1)}(k)\). Expanding (C.46) for small nonzero \(|k\Delta x|\) with \(\gamma_2(k\Delta x)^2\checkmark 1\), we obtain

\(\mathrm{Re}\Lambda_0^{(1)}(k)=-\frac{2\nu}{C_{M+1}(2-\nu)^2}\left[(4-\nu)+2\gamma_2(2-\nu)\right]k^2\Delta x+O((k\Delta x)^4).\) (42)

Since the leading-order term of \(\mathrm{Re}\Lambda_0^{(1)}(k)\) is negative for \(0<\nu<1\) and \(\Lambda_0^{(0)}(k)\) is positive, the amplification factor \(|\Lambda_0(\varepsilon,k)|\) increases towards \(|\Lambda_0^{(0)}(k)|\) as \(\varepsilon\) decreases. As a result, for a smaller Knudsen number, one needs to increase \(\gamma_2\) to reduce \(|\Lambda_0^{(0)}(k)|\) and make \(\mathrm{Re}\Lambda_0^{(1)}(k)\) more negative in order to maintain the same convergence factor. This explains the observation in \[23\].

### 3.3. Motivation for an improved hydrodynamic solver

The preceding analysis identifies the remaining bottleneck of the FIM method: the hydrodynamic stage aims to solve the system (28) with SGS iterations, but the number of iterations still depends strongly on both the Knudsen number and the grid resolution. To overcome these limitations, we seek a more efficient solver for the hydrodynamic stage that can achieve the effect of a large \(\gamma_2\) in only a few iterations. Since the actual hydrodynamic system (10) is nonlinear, we will apply Newton’s method to achieve fast convergence. The linear system arising in each Newton iteration is then solved using a multigrid method to efficiently reduce errors over a broad range of spatial frequencies and mitigate the deterioration of convergence under grid refinement.

## 4. Improved FIM method

Based on the considerations above, we now develop the improved FIM method for the full nonlinear high-order moment system (17). Before introducing the Newton-multigrid iteration for the hydrodynamic equations, we first present an IMEX scheme to address the stiffness of the Shakhov collision term in the moment stage.

### 4.1. IMEX scheme for the Shakhov model

Since the collision term is not taken into account in determining the relaxation parameter \(\omega\) by (19), the Richardson iteration (18) may become unstable as the collision term becomes increasingly stiff with decreasing _Kn_. To alleviate this stiffness, we follow the IMEX framework in \[23\] to treat the Shakhov collision term implicitly and the convection term explicitly, which yields

\(f_i^{n+1}-\omega\mathcal{Q}\left(f_i^{n+1}\right)=f_i^n-\omega\mathcal{A}_i\left(\mathbf{f}^n\right),\) (43)

where A_<sub>i</sub>_(**_f_**_<sup>n</sup>_) denotes the remaining part of -R_<sub>i</sub>_(**_f_**_<sup>n</sup>_), namely, the contribution from the spatial discretization of the convection term. Using the truncated expansions (12) and (13), the above equation can be written as

\(\sum_{|\alpha|\le M}\left(f_{i,\alpha}^{n+1}-\omega\mathcal{Q}_{i,\alpha}^{n+1}\right)\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[u_i^{n+1},\varrho_i^{n+1}]}(\mathbf{v})=\sum_{|\alpha|\le M}g_{i,\alpha}\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[u_i^n,\varrho_i^n]}(\mathbf{v}).\) (44)

Here, \(g_{i,\alpha}\) denotes the coefficient obtained from the right-hand side of (43), while the Hermite expansion coefficients \(\mathcal{Q}_{i,\alpha}^{n+1}\) of the Shakhov collision term are given according to Appendix A by

\(\mathcal{Q}_{i,\alpha}^{n+1}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
0, & \text{if}|\alpha|=0,1, \\
\bar{\nu}_i^{n+1}\left(\frac{1-\mathrm{Pr}}{5}q_{i,j}^{n+1}-f_{i,\alpha}^{n+1}\right), & \text{if}\alpha=2e_k+e_j,k,j=1,2,3, \\
-\bar{\nu}_i^{n+1}f_{i,\alpha}^{n+1}, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{array}\right.\) (45)

Multiplying both sides of (44) by \(\left(1,\nu,|\nu|^2\right)^\mathsf{T}\) and integrating over the velocity space, we obtain

\(f_{i,0}^{n+1}=g_{i,0},u_i^{n+1}=u_i^n+\frac{1}{g_{i,0}}\left(g_{i,e_1},g_{i,e_2},g_{i,e_3}\right)^\mathsf{T},\theta_i^{n+1}=\theta_i^n+\frac{2}{3}\sum_{d=1}^3\frac{g_{i,2e_d}}{g_{i,0}}-\frac{\left|u_i^{n+1}-u_i^n\right|^2}{3}.\) (46)

The right-hand side of (44) is then projected onto the same function space \(\mathcal{F}_M^{[u_i^{n+1},\theta_i^{n+1}]}\) as the left-hand side, yielding

\(\sum_{|\alpha|\le M}\left(f_{i,\alpha}^{n+1}-\omega\mathcal{Q}_{i,\alpha}^{n+1}\right)\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[u_i^{n+1},\theta_i^{n+1}]}(\nu)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le M}\tilde{g}_{i,\alpha}\mathcal{H}_\alpha^{[u_i^{n+1},\theta_i^{n+1}]}(\nu),\) (47)

with \(\tilde{g}_{i,\alpha}\) denoting the coefficients after projection. Substituting (45) into (47) and matching the coefficients gives

\(f_{i,\alpha}^{n+1}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\tilde{g}_{i,\alpha}, & \text{if}|\alpha|=0,1, \\
\frac{1}{1+\omega\bar{\nu}_i^{n+1}}\left(\tilde{g}_{i,\alpha}+\omega\bar{\nu}_i^{n+1}\frac{1-\mathrm{Pr}}{5}q_{i,j}^{n+1}\right), & \text{if}\alpha=2e_k+e_j,k,j=1,2,3, \\
\frac{1}{1+\omega\bar{\nu}_i^{n+1}}\tilde{g}_{i,\alpha}, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{array}\right.\) (48)

where the updated heat flux is obtained from (7) as

\(q_{i,j}^{n+1}=\frac{2\tilde{g}_{i,3e_j}+\sum_{d=1}^3\tilde{g}_{i,2e_d+e_j}}{1+\omega\bar{\nu}_i^{n+1}\mathrm{Pr}}.\)

One step of the above IMEX scheme is summarized in **Algorithm 2**. The implicit treatment of the Shakhov collision term improves the numerical stability of the moment iteration, whereas the computational cost per iteration remains essentially the same as that of the Richardson iteration (18).

## 4.2. Newton-multigrid iteration for hydrodynamic equations

To further enhance the efficiency and robustness of the FIM method, the time-integration-based schemes for the hydrodynamic equations, namely (24) and its SGS version, Hydro-SGS (25), are replaced by a Newton-multigrid method. Following \[31-33\], the Newton iteration leads to the linearization

\(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}(i)}\frac{\partial\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}\left(U^m\right)}{\partial U_j}\delta U_j^m=-\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}\left(U^m\right),\) (50)

where I(_i_) is the set of the indices for the cells related to the computation of the local residual \(\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}\left(\mathbf{U}^m\right)\). Once the Newton correction \(\delta U_i^m\) is obtained, the solution is updated by \(U_i^{m+1}=U_i^m+\tau\delta U_i^m,\) (51) where \(\tau\) is a relaxation parameter often set as 1. The closed-form expression of the Jacobian \(\partial\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}/\partial U_j\) can be obtained by the chain rule, but the result is usually complicated and depends on the choice of the numerical flux and the implementation of boundary conditions. Therefore, instead of deriving the Jacobian analytically, a numerical differentiation method is applied to evaluate the entries of the Jacobian matrix as \(\frac{\partial\mathcal{R}_{i,l}^\mathrm{hydro}\left(\mathbf{U}^m\right)}{\partial U_{j,k}}\approx\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(\mathcal{R}_{i,l}^\mathrm{hydro}\left(\mathbf{U}^m+\epsilon\mathbf{e}\right)-\mathcal{R}_{i,l}^\mathrm{hydro}\left(\mathbf{U}^m\right)\right),\) (52) where \(\partial\mathcal{R}_{i,l}^\mathrm{hydro}/\partial U_{j,k}\) denotes the derivative of the _l_th component of the vector \(\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}\) with respect to the _k_th component of the vector _Uj_. The unit vector **_e_** is of the same length as **_U_**, with its only non-zero entry positioned where _Uj,k_ appears in **_U_**. The parameter \(\epsilon\) is given by \(\epsilon=\epsilon_1U_{j,k}^m+\epsilon_2\), where the scale factor \(\epsilon_1=10^{-6}\) and the small perturbation \(\epsilon_2=10^{-8}\). Since the Jacobian matrix may be singular, a suitable regularization is necessary to improve the robustness of the linear solver. Unlike the problems considered in \[31-33\], the hydrodynamic system (10) is not closed by itself but relies on the constitutive variables \(\sigma\) and **_q_** provided by the high-order moment solution. These variables depend implicitly on the Knudsen number _Kn_, and the resulting hydrodynamic system therefore inherits this dependence. Accordingly, in addition to the regularization based on the \(\ell^2\) norm of the local residual, _Kn_ is also incorporated into the regularization, leading to the following modified Newton iteration \(\eta\left(Kn+\|\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}\left(\mathbf{U}^m\right)\|_\ell^2\right)\delta U_i^m+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}\left(i\right)}\frac{\partial\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}\left(\mathbf{U}^m\right)}{\partial U_j}\delta U_j^m=-\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}\left(\mathbf{U}^m\right),\) (53) where \(\eta\) is a positive constant parameter and is set to 4 in the numerical tests unless otherwise specified. Combining (53) on all cells, a linear system for all the unknowns over the computational domain can be rewritten as \(\mathbf{J}\delta\mathbf{U}^m=-\mathbf{R}^m,\) (54) where **_J_** is the regularized Jacobian matrix, and \(\delta\mathbf{U}^m\) and **_R_**_m_ are vectors of \(\delta U_i^m\) and \(\mathcal{R}_i^\mathrm{hydro}\left(\mathbf{U}^m\right)\), respectively. To solve the linear system (54) efficiently, the geometric multigrid method \[31, 34\] is adopted, with the block LU-SGS method \[35\] employed as the smoother on each grid level to damp high-frequency errors. A _V_ -cycle iteration with two pre- and post-smoothing steps is used in the implementation. The total number of grid levels is chosen such that the coarsest grid consists of 8 cells in the one-dimensional case and \(8\times 8\) cells in the two-dimensional case \[21\]. With such a coarsest grid, the substantially reduced number of degrees of freedom (DOF) allows the problem to be solved accurately at a relatively low computational cost. One step of the Newton-multigrid method is summarized in **Algorithm 3**. The geometric multigrid method is employed as the inner linear solver in Step 2, where only a few multigrid iterations are performed. ### 4.3. FIM solvers

Incorporating the improvement strategies introduced above, we summarize a family of FIM solvers in  1, in which different numerical schemes are adopted for the moment system and the hydrodynamic equations. When the Prandtl number is set to Pr = 1 and the first-order discretization is adopted, the FIM-1, FIM-2 and FIM-3 in  1 actually correspond to the FIM solvers investigated in \[23\], among which FIM-3 was shown to achieve the highest efficiency. Therefore, in the present study for the Shakhov model, we mainly focus on FIM-3 and FIM-4 with both first- and second-order discretization, and evaluate their performance through a series of numerical experiments.

## 5. Numerical experiments

In this section, three numerical examples, i.e., the planar Couette flow, the lid-driven cavity flow and the heat transfer in a bottom-heated cavity, are carried out to assess the accuracy, efficiency, and robustness of the proposed first- and second-order FIM solvers. Throughout the experiments, argon gas is considered and the dimensionless collision frequency \(\bar{\nu}\) is given by

\(\bar{\nu}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{1}{Kn}\rho\theta^{1-w},\)

where the viscosity index is _w_=0.81. Three Knudsen numbers in the near-continuum flow regime, namely, _Kn_=0.1, 0.01, and 0.001, are considered. Following \[23\], moment systems of orders _M_=10 and 9 are employed for _Kn_=0.1, _M_=8 and 7 for _Kn_=0.01, and _M_=6 and 5 for _Kn_=0.001, which have been shown to provide sufficiently accurate approximations for the corresponding Knudsen numbers. The profiles of the dimensionless density \(\rho\), temperature \(\theta\), vertical velocity _u_<sub>2</sub> and heat flux _q_<sub>1</sub>, which are computed by the second-order FIM solver on a uniform grid with _N<sub>x</sub>=_128, are plotted in Figure 1. In the dugksFoam solver, the spatial domain of the Boltzmann-Shakhov equation is discretized using a second-order finite volume scheme, while the velocity space is represented by dimension-reduced Gauss-Hermite discrete velocity points. For the reference DUGKS computations, 100 physical-space cells are used for all three Knudsen numbers, together with \(81\times 81\) discrete velocity points for _Kn=_0.1, and \(28\times 28\) discrete velocity points for _Kn=_0.01 and 0.001. In order to verify the spatial order of accuracy, the FIM solver is run on a sequence of uniform grids with _N<sub>x</sub>_ ranging from 64 to 4096. Since the exact solution cannot be obtained analytically, the numerical solution obtained on the finest grid with _N<sub>x</sub>=_4096 for each spatial discretization is taken as the benchmark solution. On a computational grid consisting of _N<sub>x</sub>_ uniform cells, the _L_<sup>2</sup> error is defined by

\(\text{Error}=\sqrt{\Delta x\sum_{i=0}^{N_x-1}\left(\bar{m}_i-\bar{m}_i^\text{finest}\right)^2},\)

where \(\Delta x=1/N_x\), \(\bar{m}_i\) denotes the cell average of either \(\rho\) or \(\theta\) over the _i_th computational cell, and \(\bar{m}_i^\text{finest}\) denotes the corresponding cell average from the benchmark solution. The errors of the first-order and second-order schemes are displayed in Figure 2, demonstrating that the expected orders of convergence are achieved for all considered Knudsen numbers.

## 5.1.2. Performance of first-order FIM solvers

We begin by examining the first-order FIM solvers, aiming to compare their performance against that reported in [23]. The total number of iterations and the associated wall-clock time spent by FIM-3 and FIM-4, as well as the IMEX-SGS iteration, to reach steady state on the grid with _N<sub>x</sub>=_256 across three Knudsen numbers are listed in  2. It is observed that the convergence of the IMEX-SGS iteration deteriorates significantly as _Kn_ decreases toward the continuum regime, leading to a substantial increase in the total number of iterations. However, the variation in wall-clock time is much less pronounced due to the use of lower-order moment systems for smaller _Kn_.

As expected, both FIM-3 and FIM-4 improve the computational efficiency over the IMEX-SGS iteration, with FIM-4 consistently delivering the best performance. The values of \(\gamma_2\) listed in  2 have been shown in [23] to provide good performance for the corresponding Knudsen numbers. The increase in the preferred value of \(\gamma_2\) as the Knudsen number decreases is consistent with the Fourier analysis in section 3. The convergence histories in Figure 3 further show that increasing \(\gamma_2\) can effectively accelerate the convergence of FIM-3, although the additional improvement becomes limited for larger values. Meanwhile, inappropriate choices of \(\gamma_2\) and the CFL number may introduce minor oscillations in the residual decay, as also reported in [23]. Therefore, selecting \(\gamma_2\) requires a compromise between convergence efficiency and robustness, which relies on empirical tuning. In contrast, FIM-4 replaces repeated hydrodynamic iterations with one Newton-multigrid step in each alternating iteration, thereby avoiding the tuning of \(\gamma_2\). Even when compared with the carefully tuned FIM-3, FIM-4 further reduces the wall-clock time by factors ranging from approximately 1.4 to 4.0. The convergence histories in Figure 3 demonstrate that FIM-4 achieves a faster and more stable residual decay with the lowest computational cost. These results indicate that one Newton-multigrid step is sufficient to provide an effective hydrodynamic correction within the FIM framework.

## 5.1.4. Effect of the new regularization strategy

To investigate the effectiveness of the proposed regularization strategy defined in (53), FIM-4 using the proposed _Kn_-based regularization is compared with that using the original residual-based regularization for the Couette flow with _N<sub>x</sub>_=256. Since the two regularization strategies exhibit nearly identical performance at _Kn_=0.01 and 0.001, only the results at _Kn_=0.1 are reported in  4.

As shown in  4, the proposed _Kn_-based regularization has little influence on the first-order discretization, indicating that the original residual-based regularization is already sufficient. For the second-order discretization at _Kn_=0.1, it reduces the iteration number from 2949 to 1148 for _M_=10 and from 2601 to 1038 for _M_=9, corresponding to a reduction of more than 60%. The convergence histories in Figure 5 further show that the proposed _Kn_-based regularization effectively suppresses the oscillations observed with the residual-based regularization strategy and achieves faster convergence. These results suggest that the _Kn_-dependent term provides additional stabilization for the Newton system under second-order discretization. Therefore, the proposed _Kn_-based regularization is adopted in all FIM-4 computations unless otherwise stated.

Numerical solutions computed by the second-order FIM solver on the \(64\times 64\) grid are presented in Figure 6, including temperature contours and heat-flux streamlines at _Kn_=0.1, as well as velocity streamlines and normalized velocity profiles along the centerlines at both _Kn_=0.01 and 0.001. It can be seen that our results agree well with DUGKS results, validating the applicability of the moment system with moderate orders in the near-continuum flow regime.

The same flow configuration was also investigated in [23], where it was shown that the first-order FIM solver generally requires much finer grids to obtain solutions comparable with the reference results, especially in the near- continuum flow regime. At _Kn_=0.001, even with a grid of \(512\times 512\) cells, the first-order discretization still shows noticeable discrepancies in the size, location, and shape of the primary and secondary vortices compared with the second-order results, as shown in Figure 6c and 7a. ## 6. Conclusion The fast iterative moment (FIM) method developed in \[23\] provides an efficient framework for accelerating steady- state solutions of near-continuum gas flows by alternating between the high-order moment system and the consistent hydrodynamic equations. In this work, the FIM solver is extended to the Shakhov model and further improved through second-order finite volume spatial discretization, an IMEX scheme with implicit treatment of the collision term, and a Newton-multigrid hydrodynamic solver equipped with a new regularization strategy. A local Fourier analysis of a linearized one-dimensional BGK model is performed to investigate the convergence behavior of the original FIM method. The analysis reveals the need for more hydrodynamic iterations at smaller Knudsen numbers and their slower convergence on refined grids, motivating the replacement of the time-integration-based hydrodynamic solver by a Newton-multigrid method. The resulting solver also forms an integrated multilevel method, in which the FIM iteration and Newton-multigrid correction provide acceleration in the velocity and spatial spaces, respectively. Numerical experiments for planar Couette flow, lid-driven cavity flow, and heat transfer in a bottom-heated cavity demonstrate that the improved FIM solver achieves significantly enhanced efficiency and robustness, particularly at small Knudsen numbers. Generally, one Newton-multigrid step in each alternating iteration is sufficient to maintain fast convergence, thereby substantially reducing the need for case-dependent parameter tuning. The numerical results also show that the proposed solver offers a greater efficiency advantage with second-order spatial discretization than with first-order discretization at small Knudsen numbers. Overall, the proposed method provides a practical and efficient framework for steady-state computation of high-order moment systems in near-continuum gas flows. ## Appendix A.
